category.name: OT & industrial control
category.description: Incidents in operational technology: PLCs, HMIs, SCADA, safety systems, building and medical devices, where safety and process continuity come first.

playbooks.name: Unauthorized PLC logic change detected
playbooks.summary: Use when a PLC program, ladder logic block, or firmware checksum differs from the approved baseline with no matching change ticket, or an engineering tool shows an unexpected download.

preparation: Store signed golden copies of every PLC project file and firmware version offline
Enable controller change auditing in the asset management or OT monitoring platform
Document which engineering workstations are allowed to download logic to each PLC
Agree with plant operations who can authorize putting a controller into manual or hold
identification: Compare the running PLC logic against the golden project using the vendor compare tool
Pull OT monitoring alerts for program download, online edit, or mode change to the PLC
Identify the engineering workstation and user account that issued the download command
Check the change management system for any approved work order covering the PLC
Ask operators whether the process has shown setpoint drift or unusual actuator behavior
containment: Coordinate with the shift supervisor before touching the controller or its network path
Switch the PLC key switch to RUN-only to block further remote program downloads
Block the source engineering workstation at the cell or zone firewall
Place affected process loops under operator manual control if the logic is untrusted
eradication: Export and preserve the modified logic and controller diagnostic buffer as evidence
Diff the modified logic block by block to document every changed rung and tag
Reload the verified golden logic during an operations-approved window
Rotate engineering software project passwords and PLC access passwords
recovery: Run a functional checkout of interlocks and alarms with control engineers after reload
Return loops from manual to automatic one at a time under operator observation
Monitor the controller for repeat download or mode-change events for two weeks
lessons: Measure how long the unauthorized change ran before detection and why
Add a detection for PLC program downloads outside approved maintenance windows
Review whether key switch positions are verified during routine rounds
Decide whether controller-level logic signing or integrity checks can be enabled

splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=ot:alerts (alert_type="Program Download" OR alert_type="Online Edit" OR alert_type="PLC Mode Change") dest_ip=<plc_ip> | table _time src_ip src_host dest_ip alert_type protocol user | sort - _time

splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip=<plc_ip> All_Traffic.dest_port IN (102, 502, 44818, 2222) by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security host=<ews_host> EventCode IN (4624, 4648) | table _time user Logon_Type src_ip | sort - _time

playbooks.name: HMI workstation compromised or showing operator-unseen actions
playbooks.summary: Use when an HMI shows signs of compromise: unknown processes, remote control sessions, screens changing on their own, or setpoint changes no operator made.

preparation: Keep an HMI asset inventory with OS version, SCADA software version, and backup location
Stage spare HMI hardware or a preimaged VM that can replace a failed operator station
Configure the SCADA server to log every setpoint change with operator ID and station
Train operators to report screens acting on their own instead of rebooting the HMI
identification: Review the SCADA alarm and event journal for writes originating from the suspect HMI
Check the HMI for remote access tools such as VNC or RDP sessions from unknown sources
Collect running processes and autoruns from the HMI using an approved offline tool
Confirm with operators which actions on the HMI they actually performed during the shift
Determine whether other HMIs on the same SCADA server show the same indicators
containment: Move operations to a known-good HMI or local panel before isolating the suspect station
Disconnect the suspect HMI network cable at the switch after operations confirms coverage
Revoke the HMI's write privileges on the SCADA server so it can only display data
Increase field rounds to verify physical process values against displayed values
eradication: Capture a forensic disk image of the HMI before rebuilding it
Rebuild the HMI from the vendor-approved image and reapply the verified project
Reset local and domain accounts that were used on the compromised HMI
Remove any remote access software not on the approved OT software list
recovery: Validate tag mapping and screen navigation on the rebuilt HMI with a lead operator
Restore write permissions for the HMI only after control engineering sign-off
Watch the HMI's network flows for new external or cross-zone connections
lessons: Determine how the attacker reached the HMI and which zone boundary failed
Add alerting for interactive remote sessions to HMIs outside approved vendor windows
Track time from operator report to security engagement and shorten it
Review application allowlisting coverage on all operator stations

splunk.title: Remote interactive logons to HMI hosts
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security host=<hmi_host> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (3, 10) | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last by user src_ip Logon_Type | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: New processes on the HMI from Sysmon
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational host=<hmi_host> EventCode=1 | stats count by Image ParentImage User CommandLine | sort count

splunk.title: Network connections leaving the HMI to non-OT destinations

playbooks.name: Malware on an OT engineering workstation
playbooks.summary: Use when EDR, AV, or OT monitoring flags malware on a workstation that holds PLC projects and can program controllers, before it can tamper with logic.

preparation: Inventory every engineering workstation and the controllers each one can program
Keep vendor engineering software installers and license keys in an offline repository
Hash and back up PLC project folders on each workstation to an offline share weekly
Confirm the EDR agent is vendor-certified for the engineering software in use
identification: Pull the AV or EDR detection details including file path, hash, and first seen time
Check whether PLC project files on the workstation were modified after the infection time
Review the engineering software's connection history for controllers contacted since infection
Look for the same malware hash on other hosts in the OT DMZ and engineering VLAN
containment: Unplug the engineering workstation from the control network and keep it powered on
Suspend any planned PLC downloads that would use project files from this workstation
Block the workstation's MAC and IP at the OT core switch and zone firewall
Notify control engineering that projects from this host are untrusted until verified
eradication: Acquire memory and disk images before cleaning the workstation
Reimage the workstation and reinstall engineering software from the offline repository
Restore PLC project files only from the pre-infection offline backup with matching hashes
Compare every controller this workstation touched against its golden logic
recovery: Reconnect the rebuilt workstation only to its permitted engineering VLAN
Have a second engineer verify the first download from the rebuilt host
Rotate credentials stored in the engineering software for controller access
lessons: Trace the infection vector such as USB, email, or a file transfer from IT
Decide whether engineering workstations should be dedicated and non-internet facing
Add file integrity monitoring on PLC project directories
Record whether golden logic comparisons were fast enough to be routine

splunk.title: Malware detections on engineering workstations
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Malware where Malware_Attacks.dest IN (<ews_host>) by Malware_Attacks.signature Malware_Attacks.file_path Malware_Attacks.file_hash | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Same malware hash elsewhere in the OT environment
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_hash="*<file_hash>*" by Processes.dest Processes.process_path

playbooks.name: IT ransomware spreading toward OT network (OT-side response)
playbooks.summary: Use when ransomware is active on the corporate network and OT must decide whether to isolate, keep running, or shut down safely while protecting the control network.

preparation: Pre-approve an IT/OT separation procedure that names who can pull the conduit links
Document which OT functions depend on IT services like AD, DNS, licensing, or MES
Test that the plant can run in island mode without the corporate network for 72 hours
Keep offline backups of historian, SCADA servers, and domain controllers in the OT zone
identification: Confirm with the IT incident lead which ransomware strain and spread methods are in play
Review the IT/OT DMZ firewall for SMB, RDP, and WMI attempts from infected IT hosts
Check OT DMZ jump hosts and patch servers for encrypted files or ransom notes
Inventory OT systems that share domain trust or credentials with the IT domain
containment: Convene plant manager, operations, and OT security to decide on island mode
Physically disconnect the IT-to-OT DMZ links per the separation procedure
Disable the IT-to-OT domain trust and any shared service accounts
Stop file replication and historian push jobs that cross into the IT network
Decide with operations whether a controlled shutdown is safer than continued running
eradication: Scan every OT DMZ server with offline signatures for the identified strain
Rebuild any OT DMZ host that shows encryption or persistence from known-good images
Reset all passwords for OT accounts that existed in or synced from the IT domain
recovery: Keep the conduit disconnected until IT declares the corporate side clean
Restore IT/OT connectivity one approved flow at a time through the DMZ
Resume historian replication and MES integration after validating data integrity
Monitor the DMZ firewall for blocked lateral movement attempts for 30 days
lessons: Measure time from IT detection to OT isolation decision
Identify OT dependencies on IT that forced or prevented island mode
Review whether production loss came from the attack or from precautionary shutdown
Update the separation procedure with contact gaps found during the incident

splunk.title: Lateral movement protocols crossing the IT/OT boundary
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic dest_zone IN ("ot-dmz", "ot") src_zone="corp" dest_port IN (135, 139, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986) | stats count values(action) as action by src_ip dest_ip dest_port | sort - count

splunk.title: Authentication into OT from IT domain accounts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.dest_category=ot Authentication.user_category=corp by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.action

playbooks.name: Unapproved vendor remote access session into OT
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor or integrator connects to OT assets through a remote access gateway, modem, or cellular router without an approved work request or outside the agreed window.

preparation: Route all vendor OT access through a single gateway with session recording
Require a work order number and named technician before any vendor session is enabled
Maintain a list of every cellular modem and remote router installed on plant equipment
Agree contractually that vendors notify the plant before connecting
identification: Pull the remote access gateway session log for the vendor account, source IP, and targets
Check the work order system for an approved request matching the session time
Call the vendor's registered contact to confirm whether the session was theirs
Review the session recording for engineering software use or file transfers
Identify which controllers or HMIs the session reached and whether writes occurred
containment: Terminate the session in the gateway after confirming no maintenance is mid-step
Disable the vendor account and any shared credential it used
Physically disconnect any cellular modem on the target equipment if it was the path
Have operations verify the affected equipment is in a safe, known state
eradication: Compare logic and configuration of every touched asset to the approved baseline
Remove any tools or files the vendor session left on OT hosts
Issue the vendor new named, MFA-protected credentials if access continues
recovery: Re-enable vendor access only with just-in-time approval by OT operations
Require a plant engineer to observe the next vendor sessions live
Confirm the asset has run normally through at least one full production cycle
lessons: Review how the session was possible without approval and close that path
Add an alert for gateway sessions without a linked work order
Audit all vendors for shared or generic accounts
Report contract compliance gaps to procurement

splunk.title: Remote access gateway sessions by vendor accounts
splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=remote_access:session (user="vendor-*" OR user_group="Vendors") | table _time user src_ip dest_host session_id duration bytes_in bytes_out | sort - _time

splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security user=<vendor_user> EventCode IN (4624, 4625) | stats count by host Logon_Type action src_ip

playbooks.name: Safety instrumented system alert or unexpected SIS trip
playbooks.summary: Use when a safety instrumented system (SIS) controller trips, faults, changes mode, or reports a program change that cannot be explained by process conditions or maintenance.

preparation: Keep the SIS on its own network segment with no routable path from IT
Record the SIS controller's approved program version, checksum, and key switch position
Write a joint procedure with process safety engineering for suspected SIS tampering
List the plant's emergency shutdown authority and the order of safety decisions
identification: Let process safety engineers first determine if the trip was a genuine process demand
Read the SIS sequence-of-events recorder for the trip cause and first-out alarm
Check the SIS controller for program mode, key switch state, and download timestamps
Review OT monitoring for any traffic to the SIS engineering port from non-SIS hosts
Verify whether the SIS engineering workstation was powered on and logged in at trip time
containment: Keep the process in its safe state; do not reset or bypass the SIS for investigation
Physically disconnect the SIS engineering workstation from the safety network
Lock the SIS key switch in RUN and secure the key with the shift supervisor
Notify plant management and process safety that a cyber cause is being investigated
eradication: Have the SIS vendor verify program integrity against the certified safety program
Preserve controller diagnostics and engineering workstation images before changes
Reload the certified safety program if any deviation is found, following functional safety rules
recovery: Complete proof testing of affected safety functions before restart
Restart the unit only with sign-off from process safety and operations management
Increase monitoring of SIS network traffic and diagnostics for the next month
lessons: Confirm whether the SIS and BPCS shared any network, workstation, or credential
Add alerting for any SIS mode change or engineering connection
Review whether trip investigation and cyber investigation ran in parallel effectively
Report findings to the functional safety management review

playbooks.name: Anomalous Modbus or DNP3 write commands on the control network
playbooks.summary: Use when OT network monitoring sees write, control, or function codes (Modbus FC 5/6/15/16, DNP3 operate or direct operate) from unexpected sources or at unusual rates.

preparation: Baseline which masters are allowed to send write function codes to each outstation
Deploy passive OT monitoring with Modbus and DNP3 protocol decoding on SPAN ports
Map register and point addresses to physical equipment so writes can be interpreted
Enable DNP3 Secure Authentication where outstations support it
identification: List every source IP that sent write or operate function codes in the alert window
Translate the written registers or DNP3 points into the equipment and values affected
Confirm with operators whether the values written match operator commands
Check whether the source is a known SCADA master, a new host, or a spoofed address
Look for preceding read sweeps that suggest point mapping by an unknown host
containment: Block the unauthorized source at the zone firewall or industrial protocol firewall
Enable write-protection or read-only mode on the affected outstations where supported
Have operators verify field values with local gauges for the affected equipment
eradication: Locate the physical port and device behind the offending source and remove it
Restore any setpoints or registers the writes changed to engineering-approved values
Add deep packet inspection rules allowing writes only from authorized masters
recovery: Run the affected loops under observation and compare trends to pre-incident baselines
Remove temporary write-protection in step with operations once the path is closed
Keep the new protocol firewall rules in alert mode briefly before full block
lessons: Measure how long unauthorized writes went undetected
Add detection for write function codes from hosts outside the master allowlist
Review whether flat network design allowed the source to reach outstations
Document the register-to-equipment map gaps found during triage

splunk.title: Modbus write function codes by source and target
splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=zeek:modbus func IN ("WRITE_SINGLE_COIL", "WRITE_SINGLE_REGISTER", "WRITE_MULTIPLE_COILS", "WRITE_MULTIPLE_REGISTERS") | stats count min(_time) as first by id.orig_h id.resp_h func | convert ctime(first) | sort - count

splunk.title: DNP3 operate commands from non-master sources

splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=zeek:modbus func="READ_*" id.orig_h=<suspect_ip> | bin _time span=5m | stats dc(id.resp_h) as targets count by _time id.orig_h

playbooks.name: Historian server compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when the process historian shows malware, unauthorized access, tampered data, or is being used as a pivot between the IT network and the control network.

preparation: Place the historian replica in the OT DMZ so IT users never query the control zone directly
Back up historian archives and configuration to offline storage on a schedule
Document every interface feeding the historian and every consumer reading it
Forward historian OS and application audit logs to the SIEM
identification: Review historian application logs for new users, admin changes, or bulk exports
Check whether historian interface nodes initiated connections to new controllers
Compare archived tag values with field device logs to detect data tampering
Identify inbound connections to the historian from IT that bypass the DMZ replica
Look for web shells or scripts in historian web and API directories
containment: Break replication between the OT historian and the DMZ replica
Restrict historian inbound access to the interface nodes only
Tell operations and engineering that historical trends may be unreliable
eradication: Rebuild the historian server from clean media and restore configuration from backup
Restore archive files from backups taken before the earliest malicious activity
Rotate historian service accounts and interface credentials
Remove any unauthorized firewall exceptions that allowed IT-to-historian access
recovery: Backfill data gaps from interface node buffers after the rebuild
Re-enable DMZ replication and validate tag counts match on both sides
Notify regulatory reporting owners if emissions or compliance data was affected
lessons: Decide whether historian data integrity checks should be routine
Review whether the historian was dual-homed or had direct IT access
Add detections for historian bulk exports and new admin accounts
Record the effort required to rebuild archives and improve backup cadence

playbooks.name: Rogue device discovered on the control network
playbooks.summary: Use when OT asset discovery or switch logs show an unknown laptop, Raspberry Pi, wireless bridge, or cellular router connected to a control network segment.

preparation: Maintain a complete OT asset inventory with MAC, IP, switch port, and owner
Enable port security or MAC alerting on managed OT switches
Lock control cabinets and network closets and log physical key issue
Run passive OT asset discovery that alerts on new MAC or OUI addresses
identification: Record the device MAC, vendor OUI, IP, and the first time it appeared on the network
Trace the device to a switch port and physical cabinet using the switch MAC table
Review which OT assets the rogue device communicated with and over which protocols
Ask maintenance and contractors whether anyone installed temporary equipment
Check badge and camera logs for access to the cabinet before first appearance
containment: Confirm with operations that the device is not providing a needed process function
Shut the switch port or remove the device under chain of custody
Photograph the device in place, including cabling and labels, before removal
eradication: Forensically image the device storage to identify tools and collected data
Check every asset the device talked to for configuration or logic changes
Disable unused switch ports in the affected cabinet
recovery: Restore any legitimate connection that was moved to make room for the device
Repeat asset discovery across all OT segments to find similar devices
Notify law enforcement or corporate security if the device was deliberately planted
lessons: Measure detection delay between device connection and alert
Decide whether 802.1X or sticky MAC is feasible on OT switches
Tighten contractor rules on bringing network equipment into the plant
Add cabinet intrusion sensors where physical access controls failed

playbooks.name: Unauthorized change to an OT zone firewall rule
playbooks.summary: Use when a firewall between IT and OT or between OT zones gets a new any-any rule, opened port, or disabled policy with no approved change request.

preparation: Export and version control the OT firewall rulebase after every approved change
Send firewall configuration change logs to the SIEM with admin user and diff
Restrict firewall management to a dedicated admin VLAN with MFA
Define the documented allowed conduits between each OT zone
identification: Pull the firewall config audit log to find who made the change and from where
Diff the current rulebase against the last approved version in version control
Search change tickets for an approved request matching the new rule
Review traffic that matched the new rule since it was created
containment: Disable the unauthorized rule after checking no legitimate process traffic now relies on it
Lock the firewall admin account that made the change pending review
Block the source address of the admin session if it was not a known management host
eradication: Restore the last approved rulebase and verify the hash matches version control
Investigate hosts that connected through the rogue rule for compromise
Rotate firewall admin passwords and API keys
recovery: Confirm with operations that all required process flows still work after restore
Schedule a rulebase review with OT engineering for any rules found to be stale
Monitor for repeated config changes from the same admin or source
lessons: Add a SIEM alert for OT firewall config commits without a ticket reference
Review who holds OT firewall admin rights and remove unneeded ones
Decide whether two-person approval is required for OT conduit changes

splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.dest IN (<ot_firewalls>) by All_Changes.user All_Changes.action All_Changes.object _time span=1h

playbooks.name: Loss of view or loss of control at the control room
playbooks.summary: Use when operators lose HMI visibility of the process or commands stop reaching field devices, and a cyber cause has not been ruled out.

preparation: Write manual operation procedures for running each unit from local panels
Identify which loss-of-view scenarios require an immediate safe shutdown
Keep a network diagram showing every path between SCADA servers and field controllers
Stock spare switches, I/O cards, and communication modules on site
identification: Confirm with the control room lead the exact scope: which HMIs, units, and controllers
Check SCADA server health, redundancy failover status, and communication driver logs
Look for broadcast storms, ARP floods, or link flapping on the control network switches
Review OT monitoring for scans, denial of service patterns, or stop commands preceding the loss
Rule out non-cyber causes such as failed power supply, fiber cut, or license expiry
containment: Dispatch field operators to local panels and confirm safe process state first
Execute the documented safe shutdown if control cannot be restored within the limit
Isolate any host generating abnormal traffic from the control network
Fail over to the redundant SCADA server or network ring if available
eradication: Remove or rebuild any host found flooding the network or issuing stop commands
Replace failed communication modules and reload their verified configuration
Verify controller logic and firmware integrity on every affected controller
recovery: Restore view first, then confirm displayed values match field readings
Return control to the HMI unit by unit with operator acknowledgement
Hold a shift handover briefing covering residual manual workarounds
lessons: Record time in manual operation and production impact
Determine whether redundancy behaved as designed
Add alerting on SCADA communication failure rates before full loss
Run a loss-of-view tabletop with operations using this incident's timeline

playbooks.name: USB-borne malware on an air-gapped plant network
playbooks.summary: Use when malware is found on an isolated OT network that has no external connectivity, implying it arrived on removable media, a laptop, or vendor equipment.

preparation: Operate a USB scanning kiosk at the plant entrance with multiple AV engines
Issue registered, write-protected USB drives for OT file transfer
Enable USB device control or logging on OT Windows hosts where vendors allow
Keep offline AV signature update media and a process to refresh it
identification: Identify the USB device serial and the first host it was plugged into from USB logs
Collect the malicious file and run it through offline multi-engine scanning
List every OT host the same USB device or file has touched
Interview the person who brought the media in and the kiosk record for it
Check for the malware's autorun or LNK propagation artifacts on network shares
containment: Quarantine the USB device in an evidence bag and log chain of custody
Suspend all removable media use on the plant network until scoping is complete
Isolate infected hosts only after operations confirms alternate coverage
eradication: Update offline AV signatures on all OT hosts using verified clean media
Clean or reimage each infected host according to vendor-approved procedures
Remove malicious files and LNK shortcuts from OT file shares
recovery: Re-enable removable media only through the scanning kiosk and registered drives
Run a full offline scan of every OT host before declaring the network clean
Verify affected controllers' logic against the golden baseline
lessons: Determine why the kiosk or policy did not stop the media
Add detection for unregistered USB device serials on OT hosts
Review whether vendors brought laptops or media without scanning
Track how current offline AV signatures were at time of infection

playbooks.name: Building management system (BMS/HVAC) compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when a building automation server, BACnet controller, or HVAC interface shows unauthorized access, odd setpoints, or is exposed to the internet and being abused.

preparation: Inventory BMS servers, BACnet controllers, and vendor cloud connectors with owners
Separate the BMS network from corporate VLANs and block internet ingress
Identify spaces with critical environmental needs such as data centers and labs
Get facilities and the BMS integrator into the IR contact list
identification: Review BMS audit logs for logins, schedule changes, and setpoint overrides
Check the BMS web interface for internet exposure via firewall NAT rules
Look for BACnet WriteProperty or device reinitialize commands from unusual sources
Confirm with facilities which temperature, airflow, or access changes they made
containment: Remove any internet-facing NAT or port forward to the BMS
Put critical HVAC units serving data centers or labs in local hand mode
Disable compromised BMS user accounts and the integrator's shared login
eradication: Patch or upgrade the BMS server and supervisory controllers to supported firmware
Restore controller schedules and setpoints from the integrator's approved backup
Change default passwords on all BACnet and BMS field controllers
recovery: Return HVAC units to automatic control after verifying setpoints
Monitor space temperatures and alarms in critical rooms for several days
Reconnect vendor remote support only through the corporate remote access gateway
lessons: Add facility systems to the vulnerability scanning scope
Add alerting for BMS logins from outside the facilities VLAN
Clarify ownership of BMS security between facilities and IT
Require BMS integrators to use named accounts with MFA

splunk.title: Inbound internet traffic to BMS assets
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic dest_ip IN (<bms_ips>) src_zone=untrust | stats count values(dest_port) as ports by src_ip action | sort - count

splunk.title: BACnet write and reinitialize requests
splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=zeek:bacnet bvlc_function=* (pdu_service="write-property" OR pdu_service="reinitialize-device" OR pdu_service="device-communication-control") | stats count by id.orig_h id.resp_h pdu_service

splunk.title: BMS application logins by user and source
splunk.spl: index=facilities sourcetype=bms:audit action=login | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last by user src_ip result | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

playbooks.name: Medical device (IoMT) compromised or behaving abnormally
playbooks.summary: Use when a networked medical device such as an infusion pump, imaging modality, or patient monitor shows malware, unexpected traffic, or tampering, with patient safety first.

preparation: Maintain a medical device inventory with model, OS, MDS2 form, and clinical owner
Segment medical devices into VLANs by device class with deny-by-default rules
Agree with clinical engineering who can take a device out of service
Keep manufacturer security contacts and FDA recall/advisory references handy
identification: Ask clinical staff whether the device is in use on a patient right now
Have clinical engineering check the device for altered settings or drug library changes
Review network flows from the device for internet, SMB, or scanning activity
Check the manufacturer's advisories for the device model and software version
containment: Swap the device for a known-good unit before removing it from patient care
Move the device to a quarantine VLAN or disconnect it once clinically safe
Block identified malicious destinations for the whole device VLAN
eradication: Work with the manufacturer to reimage or patch the device using validated software
Do not install unvalidated EDR or patches that could void device certification
Check sibling devices of the same model for the same indicators
recovery: Have clinical engineering perform a functional and safety check before reuse
Return the device to service and monitor its traffic for a week
Inform the patient safety committee and risk management of the outcome
lessons: Evaluate whether a patient safety event report or regulator notification is needed
Add device-class traffic baselines to the IoMT monitoring platform
Review procurement requirements for supported OS and patch commitments
Track how long it took to find a replacement device

splunk.title: External connections from medical device VLANs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_zone="medical-devices" All_Traffic.dest_zone=untrust by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | sort - count

splunk.title: SMB and scanning behavior from the device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic src_ip=<device_ip> | stats dc(dest_ip) as targets values(dest_port) as ports count by src_ip | where targets > 20

splunk.title: IoMT platform alerts for the device model
splunk.spl: index=iomt sourcetype=iomt:alerts device_model="<device_model>" | stats count values(alert_name) as alerts by device_ip location

playbooks.name: Water or wastewater SCADA intrusion
playbooks.summary: Use when a water or wastewater utility sees unauthorized SCADA access, chemical dosing setpoint changes, pump changes, or remote access misuse at treatment plants or lift stations.

preparation: Set hard high/low limits on chemical dosing in PLC logic, not only on the HMI
Remove direct internet exposure of SCADA and remote access tools at plants
Keep contacts for the state drinking water primacy agency, WaterISAC, and CISA
Document manual operation procedures for each treatment process and lift station
identification: Review HMI event logs for chemical feed, pump, or valve setpoint changes
Confirm every change with the operator on duty and the chief operator
Check remote access tool logs for sessions from unknown IPs or at odd hours
Pull lab and online analyzer readings to see if water quality was affected
Identify which remote stations communicate over cellular or radio links
containment: Reverse unauthorized setpoint changes and confirm with online analyzers
Disable remote access software on SCADA hosts and switch to on-site operation
Increase manual sampling frequency until water quality is confirmed
Notify the primacy agency and leadership if public health could be impacted
eradication: Remove remote access tools not managed through a secured gateway
Reset every SCADA account, especially shared operator logins
Review PLC logic at affected stations against backups
recovery: Restore secure remote access through an MFA gateway before resuming remote operation
Continue enhanced sampling until analyzers and lab results are stable
Coordinate public communication with the utility's PIO if a notice is needed
lessons: Confirm whether PLC-level dosing limits would have prevented the change
Add alerts for setpoint changes beyond normal ranges
Report the incident to CISA and sector partners with indicators
Fund replacement of unsupported HMI operating systems

splunk.title: Chemical dosing and pump setpoint changes
splunk.spl: index=ot sourcetype=scada:events event_type="setpoint_change" (tag="*NAOH*" OR tag="*CL2*" OR tag="*PUMP*" OR tag="*FEED*") | table _time station user hmi_host tag old_value new_value

splunk.title: Remote access sessions to SCADA hosts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic dest_ip IN (<scada_ips>) app IN ("teamviewer", "anydesk", "vnc", "ms-rdp") | stats count min(_time) as first by src_ip dest_ip app | convert ctime(first)
